book: 252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam

chapters.file: ch07 - I Slippin’ Jimmy with a law degree is like a chimp with a machine gun.md

chapters.relation: Clipsham distinguishes Jimmy and Kim's 'scamming for fun' (deceiving Ken over rare tequila in 'Switch', or a montage of pointless cons in 'Marco') from the 'scheming for benefits' of Mike, Gus, and Chuck, who lie only to secure a specific end. Using Kant's prohibition on treating people merely as means, he argues that scheming for a benefit is more disrespectful than scamming for its own sake, because the latter treats a mark as an unwitting player in a game rather than a tool. He also rejects the worry that fun-scamming corrupts character, noting Jimmy was already dishonest and that Gus and Lalo's worst vices have no root in playful deception.

chapters.file: ch09 - 2. Don’t Go to Lawyers for Moral Guidance.md
chapters.relation: Ralston reads Jimmy McGill's slide into Saul Goodman as a study in moral decline, using Dewey's (and Bourdieu's) theory of habit to explain why a person capable of right action repeatedly chooses the wrong path—the pressures of criminal clients, Chuck's contempt, and HHM's rejection wear down his will as an ingrained disposition. He contrasts Kant's categorical imperative with mere 'imperatives of prudence' (rules of thumb for achieving any end), arguing Jimmy consistently follows the latter, as when he unhinges Chuck at the disbarment hearing to win. Invoking Hart's separability of law and morality and Singer on the ethicist's training, he concludes lawyers like Saul make poor moral guides.

chapters.file: ch10 - 3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty.md
chapters.relation: Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.

White uses Better Call Saul's cartel world—the 'Bagman' shootout, Mike's account of Philadelphia police corruption, Tuco's meth-driven violence—to frame the ethics of the U.S. War on Drugs, tracing its racist origins and drawing a sustained analogy to alcohol Prohibition. She marshals Mill's harm principle from On Liberty to argue adults may choose their own risks absent harm to others, making criminalization inconsistent given legal alcohol. She then fairly lays out the pro-War case (Bennett on deterrence, the Robins Vietnam-heroin study, Mill's own bar on selling oneself into slavery applied to addiction) before favoring decriminalization on the Portugal model.

chapters.file: ch12 - II You can be on one side of the law or the other.md
ch13 - 5. The Sovereign State of Salamanca.md
chapters.relation: Barta and Barnes read the show's Court and Cartel as parallel Hobbesian sovereigns. The New Mexico desert and the criminalized drug trade function as Hobbes's state of nature—lawless, where Nacho robs thieves who 'have no recourse' and Mike sticks up a mule with a garden hose—illustrating natural equality (a small man can kill a big one) and the war of all against all. From mutual fear, deals emerge (Mike and Gus's desert standoff, Mike keeping his word over twenty dollars), but 'covenants without the sword' need a Common Power: Tuco, Hector, Lalo, and ultimately Don Eladio form a feudal hierarchy enforcing loyalty by terror, just as the state's police monopoly on force sustains the Law.

chapters.file: ch14 - 6. The Morality of Mike’s Manifesto.md
chapters.relation: The Gibsons analyze Mike Ehrmantraut's code—'if you make a deal with somebody, you keep your word'—through virtue ethics and Stoicism. Aristotle's function argument and Golden Mean partly vindicate Mike's counsel toward temperance and restraint (not carrying a gun, sparing the Salamanca driver), yet Aristotle's claim that 'bad people are full of regrets' marks him as a flawed 'wicked' man given his inner turmoil over breaking his son. They read his calm as Stoic (Marcus Aurelius's Meditations on controlling the mind, Spartan simplicity), and weigh Kant's intent-based defense of his killing the dirty cops Hoffman and Fensky against Mill's social-rule view of sanctionable wrongs.

chapters.file: ch15 - 7. Saul Goodman Stands Before the Law.md
chapters.relation: Haven reads Jimmy's transformation into Saul through Kafka's parable 'Before the Law' as interpreted by Derrida. Like Kafka's man from the country waiting at a gate made only for him, Jimmy stands before 'the Law' as an inaccessible, self-deferring promise guarded by doorkeepers—Mike at the parking booth, Howard, and truly Chuck, who secretly blocks his job. Derrida's analysis of the secret as an unfulfillable promise explains the Law's contradictions (sacred yet petty, present yet silent). Haven argues Jimmy grasps the Law's dirty secret—that it 'doesn't exist' apart from its agents—and, unlike Kafka's man, chooses the liminal outlaw space of Saul Goodman rather than waiting for admittance.

chapters.file: ch16 - III Put on your big boy pants and face reality.md

chapters.relation: Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.

chapters.file: ch18 - 9. The Prequel versus Free Will.md
chapters.relation: Frim argues that Better Call Saul, precisely because it is a prequel, illustrates Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason—every event, including Walt's meth empire or Jimmy's burner-phone hustle, has a causal 'because' stretching infinitely back—and thus a deterministic universe. He dismantles the appeal to Heisenberg/quantum indeterminacy (randomness is not free choice) and refutes three myths: that determinism is boring (the causal 'Story One' is far more gripping than the free-will 'Story Two'), amoral (murder is wrong for its effects; we can keep 'suffering' and drop 'guilt'), and mindless (Nacho's ordered mind versus Tuco's drug-addled one shows minds function well or badly). He enlists Socrates' 'no one goes willingly toward the bad' to recast wrongdoing as disordered reasoning.

Šekrst uses Jimmy's many personas—Slippin' Jimmy, James McGill, Saul Goodman, Viktor St. Clair, Gene Takavic—to survey theories of personal identity. She shows psychological continuity (Locke's memory-based view) falters on sleep, comas, and Chuck's apparent dementia, and the brute-physical/bodily view falters on brain-transplant thought experiments and the Phineas Gage case ('no longer Gage'). She defends a narrativist account with a reality constraint: identity is the story one is disposed to tell about oneself, so Jimmy can disown Slippin' Jimmy and reidentify as Saul, and Gene can recall his Saul self—narrative being sufficient though perhaps not necessary for persistence, with others' stories contributing but the protagonist's being authoritative.

Doll analyzes self-deception across the series using Gregg Ten Elshof's four mechanisms—attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, and rationalization. Chuck's electromagnetic hypersensitivity is a real psychological condition about which he deceives himself as to its physical cause, reinforced by everyone accommodating him; his refusal to see Jimmy as anything but 'Slippin' Jimmy' is rationalized as protecting others while sabotaging his brother. Jimmy, via perspective-shifting through Chuck's eyes, comes to believe he can only be Slippin' Jimmy, then rationalizes the Saul persona. Drawing on Joseph Butler and Adam Smith, Doll argues self-deception blinds moral judgment and is ultimately Saul's undoing, leaving him alone in hiding.

chapters.file: ch21 - IV Confidence is good—facts on your side, better.md
ch22 - 12. A Cave of His Own Making.md
chapters.relation: Golden reinterprets Plato's Allegory of the Cave to argue Chuck enslaves himself in a 'cave of his own making'—his hypochondriacal electromagnetic hypersensitivity—to keep Jimmy accountable and to exact vengeance for Jimmy's unpunished childhood thefts. Using Aristotle's De Anima psychology and the function argument, he places Chuck's imagination (phantasia) below reason: Chuck retains the rationality to serve clients like Mesa Verde and to detect Jimmy's document fraud, but sinks below the Golden Mean into the vices of meanness (short of kindness) and cowardice (short of courage) toward his brother. He adds Kierkegaard's Repetition: Chuck is stuck in backward-looking 'recollection' of vengeance and cannot make the forward, committed 'repetition' of simply being Jimmy's brother.

holes.name: Self-Deception
holes.what: The paradoxical condition of being both the deceiver and the deceived, holding a false belief one is motivated not to recognize as false, via attention management, procrastination, perspective shifting, or rationalization.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is built entirely around self-deception as a distinct problem (Ten Elshof, Joseph Butler, Adam Smith) that the taxonomy has no dedicated slug for; Sartre's 'bad-faith' is only an approximate neighbor and no philosopher slug exists for Butler.
